doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 5, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]

title: First hearing Bird and Diz on furlough and learning bebop language
summary: Gibbs heard Dizzy and Parker while on Army furlough, took Dizzy's syncopation, and after the Army learned bebop language, harmony and technique.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Okay. Well speaking of ideas, you wrote that when you first tried to play bebop early on that your first note and your last note would be right, and everything in the middle was very questionable.

Well you’ve got to understand, when I first heard Bird and Diz I was home on furlough. And when I heard — I didn’t believe what I was hearing. But I know they were playing double-time, and I was in the Army by the way, I was on furlough. And in the Army I was the drummer with a 38-piece orchestra making all the Army movie pictures. We had a number of drummers in the band so we used to have little jam sessions and I would play vibes, with some of the other drummers playing. And I played straight ahead, you know. But I came back from furlough and went to jam with the guys, hearing Dizzy Gillespie I got the syncopation from Dizzy. Because if you heard Dizzy play and took the notes away [scats]. So I got the syncopation and noticed that Charlie Parker played — he had to © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

be George Gershwin. Because everything he played was a song. Everything that came out of that horn, you slow it down and you could write a lyric to it. So my point, getting back to that first note, I heard all those notes so I wanted to play them but I didn’t know what the heck they were doing, so I said the first note I hit was always boom — and I ended up on saying boom. In the middle is [inaudible]. The rhythms were there but not the notes until I came out of the Army and started jamming with players who were learning, like I was, and I would go down to hear Bird and Diz and I was lucky that I learned the bebop language fast. You know I picked up what Dizzy did with the rhythms and the chord changes of the song. Everything was a little different. You know in those days when you played with big bands and you’re a jazz player, you had to read music or play the same. Here, with this, you had to have technique, really have technique, you had to be like a classically trained whatever you were playing. Because to play all those notes you had to play your instrument that well. And then you had to know harmony and theory inside out to see how they were going through the chord changes, how they were, even you take one chord like if anybody knows what a C7 is, they could make four chords out of a C7. You could take four different chords and play on the C7 where it would all fit. You wouldn’t be out. It would all be in notes you know?
